title: Ender's Game
review:
If you want to start reading again this is my go-to recommendation. This thing is so fun and fast paced, with some cool sci-fi ideas. And it's pretty short. You could read this in a weekend easy. Humanity was attacked by aliens, thousands of people died in this war, until the aliens were repelled by a mysterious attack by a lone human ship. Humanity, still recovering from the last war, wants to strike back before the aliens can regroup and attack again. So they create a dangerous children's military training school to train the next generation of generals.

Our protagonist Ender rises to the top of this school with his tactical genius. One standout is a zero-gravity combat training exercise where Ender tells him teammates to put your feet toward the enemy. If you face the enemy head-on you'll think of this as a 2D battlefield, but with your feet toward the enemy you'll think in 3-dimensions, and as a bonus your legs will shield you from enemy stunners.

And of course the book has a couple really cool sci-fi twists that I won't mention here.

title: Speaker for the Dead
review:
While this is a sequel to Ender's Game, it's actually the book Orson Scott Card wanted to write from the beginning. Originally Ender's Game was just a prologue that expanded into an entire novella. This is very funny because while Ender's Game became a smash hit, it is nothing like this book. Fans of the first book are in for some serious whiplash. Previous book was short and pacey, this is slow and thoughtful. Previous protagonist was a tactical genius general, now he's a traveling pastor. Previous book had twists and reveals, this one has one inevitable ending broadcast from page 1.

Fun Fact: this was the first book I read with special relativity as a central plot point. You see Ender now gives eulogies after people die, but he doesn't sugar-coat their life. He tells their life as it actually was; warts and all to give closure. After an abusive father dies, the crying daughter sends a message out requesting Ender to give one of his eulogies. Ender receives that request, but it will take him time to reach the planet. Due to relativity, it will take a week for him but a decade for the girl. So when Ender arrives the girl is now a fully grown adult that wishes she never requested Ender at all. Now Ender is in the middle of terribly broken family with a horrible festering wound never healed that the father left. What is he supposed to do? Can he really help when so much hurt has happened? It's a really gripping tragedy, but absolutely nothing like the previous book.

title: There is no Antimemetics Division
review:
This really shows the best parts of SCP. It's so weird and creative. Unlike most horror, this feels like something that could've only been written in the 21st century. It's just so out there.

The book is about 'antimemes', SCPs that remove themselves from your memory. Stuff like The Silence in Doctor Who: when you stop looking at them you immediately forget they ever existed. How do you fight something like that? Answer: be really smart.

Like the best sci-fi novels, every chapter in this book gives an idea that could carry an entire series on its own, and then moves on to something even more crazy and out there. I was really surprised how much ideas kept escalating in this book. Ngl all this escalating probably made this thing hype af to read as it was being released on the SCP wiki back in 2015.

And this book is scary. I got really spooked by it. I had such a good time with this book I finished it in two days. The best SCP authors always have the most inventive stories, and it really pisses me off that more of them havn't made the jump into traditional publishing yet, so it's going to be a while before we get another book like this one again.

title: Project Hail Mary
review:
Im gonna have a hard time watching this movie in a few months because the protagonist in my head looks nothing like Ryan Gosling.

This author is just so wholesome. He just loves science in this pure and amateur way. You know he follows NASA on Twitter and loves talking about fun science facts.

The Martian was just a series of unique science problem -> fun science solution -> problem -> solution etc for the whole thing. That book was great, but this one's plot has a little more sauce. More character and more emotional moments. Nothing crazy, just more to spice things up. Another big difference from The Martian is this book's science is a lot more out there. For me it was always in the realm of possibility, but there might be a few too many crazy ideas for some people. This book is about 1/3 flashback, especially early on. My theory is the movie is only going to have 3 total flashback scenes.

It was a lot easier and breezy than The Remains of the Day. If you want to get back into reading this might be what gets you started. Fun science romp.

title: The Blade Itself (The First Law: Book 1)
review:
This thing really ends with anti-climax; that's both my opinion and what both my friends who read this said. You'll put this book down not saying 'wow that was so good' you'll say 'I'm excited to see what happens next' and there's a pretty big difference there.

I think even hardcore fans of this series agree this first book is kinda pointless; it's a setup for book 2. But, that didn't mean I didn't have a good time with it. I actually enjoyed this book cover-to-cover. The plot was always moving and it felt like important things were happening.

Here's what I mean: one character's (Jezel's) whole story is trying to win the king's tournament. We follow his training with everyone doubting him because he doesn't stand a chance against his rival. But Jezal has a good master so maybe he can win? This is a classic plot. So after spending the whole book rooting for this guy we finally start the tournament at the end. And Jezal only wins the tournament because someone cheated on his behalf. So he wins the tournament through foul play. And at the feast afterward the author gives us a ton of purposely gross and anticlimactic language. Joe Abercrombie is purposely deflating this important thing he spent the whole book building up. Does that retroactively make the rest of the book bad, even if you never bored? I don't think so.

Of course I can't mention this book without bringing up Glotka; everyone who reads this book also falls in love with this character. This horribly bitter cripple who makes a living torturing people, he is just amazing. Literally every chapter focusing on him is great. Abercrombie really knows how to make enchanting characters.

title: Before They are Hanged (The First Law: Book 2)
review:
I thought the anticlimax of the first book was a fluke, this is when i realize it would be Joe Abercrombie's modus operandi. Everything in this world just sucks. The supposedly elite kingsguard? They shake in their boots when a real fighter shows up. The grand university staffed by old scholars? It's full of a bunch of bickering old people living in a gross dungeon. The ancient bridge made by a bygone civilization? The sheer un-naturalness of it makes everyone want to leave as quickly as possible. Nothing in this world is cool. Nothing is grand. The less you experience of this world the better, probably better to just stay home instead of this grand quest our protagonists get up to.

This world sucking does make it all feel more 'real' though. Like, because everything sucks you see our own world in its reflection. Nothing here is larger than life. The downside of this tone is that nothing is every satisfying. The finales of both this and the last book were both real wet farts. Like I said these books are engaging the whole time, but they never leave you feel satisfied when you put them down. I still love Glotka though, best character. In this book that poor cripple oversees the defense of a doomed city where no one expects him to succeed. I won't spoil it but if you've been paying attention to Abercrombie's tone you can probably guess what happens.

title: The Last Argument of Kings (The First Law: Book 3)
review: You know, part of me was holding out hope for a satisfying ending in the third book. Fool me 3 times shame on me I guess; satisfaction just isn't Abercrombie's style. But also, like usual, I was still engaged cover to cover. I still just am never left with the warm feeling I normally get when I finish a good book. At least Glotka continues to be a best character of all time. I'll also give a shoutout to Bayaz: he's ostensibly a kind Gandalf-y ancient wizard, but he becomes more and more sinister as the series goes on. He's kinda boring in the first book, and by book 3 he is full on series antagonist and I'm so on board. I also really like what Abercrombie did with him going forward. In The First Law Bayaz was a pretty central character, staying at the center of every plot point. For the later books though, Bayaz has melted into the shadows, becoming a puppet-master. Now he only shows up like once a book to scare the crap out of other characters. Whenever he shows his bald face it's always a highlight of the given book. In this form the character just feels so much more powerful. He's like a wizardly Freddy Krueger.

title: Best Served Cold (World of The First Law: Book 1)
review:
This is fantasy Kill Bill. We have a badass female protagonist, they are left for dead in a bloody opening betrayal scene, she swears revenge as she claws her way out, the book is mostly her taking killing people one by one as she works her way up the hierarchy, each killing is more brutal and violent than the last, until at the end she comes face to face with the ringleader who caused all this and she kills him too. And you know what? This book is really good.

For the record none of that was spoilers, this is all stuff you could guess from chapter 1. That's just the structure, the meat of the book is how good these characters are to watch. Characters continues to be Abercrombie's specialty. He gives us a little team each with their own complex relationship with each other and weird character quirks. I could see a dozen people reading this book and each rooting for a different person: maybe the extravagant poison master, or his cute apprentice who knows more than she lets on. Maybe like me you'll love the son of a legendary barbarian that is trying to just do the right thing, or maybe you'll just love the autistic psychopath. The team gets in a lot of messes and they all have their moments to endear you to them.

Abercrombie's dark tone is the darkest its ever been here. There's a couple deaths I can still remember in vivid detail a year after reading it. The worst ones have that awful moment right before they die where you think 'wait, maybe they don't deserve this. stop.' and then they are killed. These tragedies can really stick with you, which can be a hard thing to do. It's easy to go numb reading a dark fantasy story, just letting it all slide by. But Abercrombie pulls you in, these are not soft and impotent tragedies, they stick deep in your heart and fester there. If you like darkness there's a lot of like here. This was my favorite book by Abercrombie, at least until I'd read his next book: The Heroes. But I like The Heroes more for personal reasons, this is still probably the objectively best book by him I've read.

title: The Heroes (World of the First Law: Book 2)
review:
This is by far my favorite book by Abercrombie, but it's probably because it was the right book at the right time. It has its merits though, this book is probably the closest thing to proper literature Abercrombie's ever written if this was a historical setting instead of a fantasy one I could see this being read in high school English classes. Ok, but what is this book about? This book is about a single fantasy battle. Not a war, literally just one battle. It's 500 pages long and has a map in the front.

So the book has an enormous cast of characters, on both sides of the battle. We spend a lot of time talking about hopes, fears, and backstories, and lots of time talking about what the purpose of the war is. Then the plot of the book is basically our giant cast of characters getting killed off one after another, usually related to facts only tangientially related to the enemy they are supposed to be fighting. Along the way the book takes every opportunity to explore random little moments in the battle. One standout point is a self-contained chapter where we jump perspective between two-dozen people in a skirmish, where we jump right when our narrator dies, to the person who killed them. It's one of those sequences where it gets strangely more satisfying the longer it goes on because it loops around from being a little tedious by the fourth jump to being really entertaining by the twentith.

When the book is over our once full cast has been measurably cut down, and the survivors are now all looking at each other like
. Was it all worth it? Think about all the people who died, should we say something? Should we do something?

title: Steelheart (Reckoners: Book 1)
review:
POV you are me in 2020 and thought The Boys was boring, kinda gross, and a little ugly. BUT, you really like the premise: 'normal people trying to kill superheroes' is just cool. So, someone recommends this book that has one key difference from The Boys: this is not written by someone exacting some weird revenge on a genre that took over their industry, this writer actually likes normal superhero stories and isn't afraid to deliver on actually cool superhero fights.

The main plot of the book is trying to kill a team of supervillains, who all same a single weakness. The weakness could be anything: you can only hurt them if you've seen their face, their powers only work at night, they are weak to Cool-Aide. The protagonists study the habits of these people to try and figure out what their weakness is, and then there's a showdown where they use the weakness to try and kill them, and of course something goes wrong and they need to invent a new plan on the fly. This was the first thing I read by Sanderson and I loved it for all the standard Sanderson hallmarks: deep magic system, developed world, medium-to-good characters, and of course an absolutely explosive series of twists and action in the finale.

title: The Way of Kings (Stormlight Archives: Book 1)
review:
I liked this book but not because it's good, I just really liked the concept of Kaladin's character. Kaladin's dad was a doctor training up his son to follow in his footsteps, but Kaladin wanted to be a solider. So Kaladin runs away and squanders the good life his father tried to build for him, Kaladin is then captured and sold as a slave. The man trained for a noble profession, makes a mistake and now is at the lowest rung of society. It almost didn't matter what Kaladin actually did from this point on, I was carried on that alone. And it's good I liked Kaladin because I'm pretty sure that of the four main narrators in this series he gets the most screentime. The others are cool too though: we also have a disgraced aristocrat pretending to be a scholar to steal a jewel from the king's daughter and save her own house, we have an assassin who killed the former king on the run and full of guilt, and the dead king's brother obsessed with virtue and tradition while the court plays politics around him. We have to have four narrators you see, because this is the beginning of Sanderson's giant epic-scale fantasy story. This is his Wheel of Time, his Elric, his Lord of the Rings. However, in the years since reading this I've wondered if Sanderson isn't cut out for this scale of storytelling.

There's a lot going on here, it's dangerous trying to punch at this weight class. It's very easy to let this story slip away from you or become boring. This is where Sanderson will really prove his long-form writing chops, and already I think this story would've been better just focusing on two characters instead of tour. Sanderson has done everything you're supposed to do, he paces it such that the boring part of one character's story we are at a high moment of another's, he's built a giant world, set up a ton of mysteries, but I don't think this book is as good as it needs to be to kick off a story like this. Despite my criticism, when I'd first read this book I called it my favorite book of all time so it has to be at least ok. The issues with this series wouldn't be seen for me until the later books.

title: Words of Radiance (Stormlight Archives: Book 2)
review:
Online folks call this the peak of the series, which is really ominous because this is where I started to see cracks forming. The positives of this book are obvious: Kaladin is struggling whether he wants to serve the nobility, Shallan is becoming a full con-artist, Adolin goes from snotty brat to relatable main character. These are very cool plot points, and I love that our POV characters are now crossing over with each other, but this book is really dragged down by it's really slow buildup. We get like 80 pages of nothing interesting happening at any given time before the next action sequence. It's not even that the plot is slow, it's just boring. The highs are great (Kaladin saving Adolin during his duel is the only one I can still remember but I assume there were more), but the buildups are too long.

Also, the ending of this book... idk I think I heard an dark thunderclap when I finished reading because this new status quo does not excite me for the future. I feel the next book with all these new Knight Radiant standing around is going to be so boring. At of time of writing I haven't read book 3 yet. I hope these fears end up unwarranted.

title: Shadow and Bone (Shadow and Bone: Book 1)
review:
I didn't finish a single book in February, despite reading more total in February than January. And then I finished this book in 4 days. Whoops. But can you blame me? It's a YA novel with two love interests, in a school, with a rags to riches peasant girl. Be still my beating heart!

I'd already read the authors next series (Six of Crows). The setting and plot of this are only 30% as interesting and everything feels more generic. I can't tell if this is just Bardugo in her unformed larval stage, or whether she used something more tried and true to break into the industry? Could be both. Six of Crows was a rag-tag group of people conning their way across the world to do a heist. This is self insert protagonist being the hero of the prophecy and learning to harness her special powers that no one else has. But I still had a great time reading it. If we judge books by whether I finish them Bardugo is a greater writer than Borges, Flannery O'Connor, and C.S. Lewis.

In terms of pure enjoyment, I had a better time reading all four books I started in February vs this one. This one was very easy to read, but it's all in one ear out the other. This book was like popcorn. Maybe the book equivalent is YouTube vs movies. One is just easier to consume for long periods of time.

But lets not forget; this proves you never age out of YA. Hot boys are forever. (And the boys are really hot)

(And for the record, the twist in the 3rd act got me. I predicted it wrong)

title: Blessed Are You
review: I've read this probably half a dozen times cover to cover. It's a short book about the Beatitudes that I keep finding pearls in. The best Franciscan writers have this eternal quality where they where they invite you to not just move onto the next thing, but meditate on the same truths over and over. When I worked manual labor I could pick up this book in the morning, read a single page, and then chew on that page all day. Fun fact: my first tattoo was inspired by this book. It's easy to eat a fish, tearing big chunks of meat off its bones, but takes serious skill to cleanly remove all the meat from the fish.

title: Listening At Prayer
review:
This is a very short book on prayer written by one of the founders of the CFRs, you might know them the extremely radical order of franciscans that also make music and have a podcast. I'm gonna be real: it's really weird listening to a podcast recorded by people who live in the conditions they do.

Anyway about the book: it's not very long, and the writing isn't very deep. But what you come to franciscan writing for is the really simple things. It's a book written by an incredibly holy man, for lay people, about how to be silent and listen for God's voice in prayer. This book is so simple it feels weird even writing a review for it.

title: Happy Are You Poor
review: This is the gold standard for living biblical poverty, and it does not mince words. This is a dangerous book to read if you feel secure in the way you're living out poverty in your life. Christ very explicitly says that wealth hinders spiritual growth. Poverty is not just for some people, it's for everyone. Thomas Dubay's writing is so systematic and academic that it feels like he closing off any possible chance of escape for his reader. No one puts down this book and feels lukewarm about living a life of poverty, and he does this all without being weird and crafting some mythology about poverty. It's just straight facts of being Christian.

title: The Fire Within
review: This is a 500 page book diving into The Interior Castle by Theresa of Avila and Dark Night of the Soul by John of the Cross. These are two extremely influential mystics whom God gifted extreme experiences of contemplation. If an extremely deep dive on this sounds interesting I'd recommend it, otherwise don't bother. Dubay writes like an academic though, so even though the subject matter is extremely mystical, you can still treat this book like an academic thing and just skip to the chapters you're interested in. Something I continue to think about is how Theresa of Avila describing others who had these extreme experiences, and mostly uses examples of lay people when discussing the most extreme states (she doesn't use examples of priests of nuns of whatever) implying these extreme forms of prayer are possible for anyone if God wills it.

title: Watchmen
review:
The funniest thing about Watchmen is that tons of people on reddit rank it as their #1 comic of all time, so some people read it as their first ever comic with the logic 'well if i'm gonna read a comic i might as well read the best one', but Watchmen does not make a great introduction to comics. I know this happens because this is what I did.

What makes Watchmen amazing is how it's in conversation with the rest of the industry, playing with and subverting tropes while pushing the boundary of what's possible in the medium. Ngl thought, many of the ways it's amazing I still only half understand. I did still have a good time with it. I really liked prose between chapters building out the world. One smaller detail I like is that comics exist in this universe, but instead of superheroes the comic depict pirate stories.

title: The Remains of the Day
review:
This protagonist broke my heart. Stevens is a butler reflecting on his life, and his first person perspective gives the book such an irony. His life is so sad, but he doesn't see it that way. He's actually quite proud of his career, serving the great Lords and Ladies of Britain. But his employers never thank him, and he has paid such a price to do this job well. First off he has no friends. At one point he remarks 'a butler is only off-duty when they are alone.' And the person he most could've become friends with (Miss Kenton) he frequently hurts in unintentional ways because of his devotion to his job. So many times he leaves her in tears and he is wondering why she is so unprofessional. It hurts so much seeing how much he hurts her and he refuses to see he's even done it. The irony of Stevens's life is most obviously seen when we learn his Lord was a Nazi sympathizer in WWII. Stevens was at least taking consolation in serving a great man, except he wasn't. And he seems to have blocked from his mind him being a bad man.

Every time I picked up this book i'd read a section and think 'I have to mention this in the review.' The book is so dense with chapters i'll remember the rest of my life.

This book is so sad, but it doesn't get there by killing baby goats or blowing up orphanages. The painful sorrow is from one guy, talking about his sad life, and being proud of it. There's one heartaching moment near the end where it seems for a second Stevens will learn his lesson, but then he doesn't. This book was beautiful. I see why it won a Nobel Prize in literature.

title: The Galton Case
review:
I paid $5 for this book at a thrift store knowing nothing about it. I read it completely blind except the fact that a talking head recommended the author. This is a noir detective book from the 50s originally published as a cheap paperback. These things are meant to be read by men on the bus on the way to work. We got women in tight shirts, gangsters, rich families, a couple action scenes. Your grandparents would've loved this book. Due to this purpose, the book has a kinda odd structure. Each chapter is like 4 pages long and they are all the same. The detective shows up somewhere, talks to a tropey character, and gets information to set up the next location with a new tropey character in it for next chapter. The book always felt in motion, but never felt it was going somewhere interesting. By the end I really liked the story, but I wondered what the purpose was in the middle. I think mostly that was the structure just feeling odd to me. Also the protagonist is nothing. He's not a character. I've previously said the key to a mystery is good characters. That's not the case here, so why did I finish it? Because the prose and theme are really good. We are dealing with a family in shambles because of a rebellious son being cast out of the family. And the book explores the wake this event, all the people hurt and all the people trying to take advantage of it. And these sentences really feel so good to read. It's just cover to cover amazing writing. Actually, here's a bit of writing I just found by flipping to a random page.

“Why did you do it?” I said.

'I don’t know. I guess I just got sick of him. Now it’s time for me to take my punishment. I killed, and I deserve to die.'

The tragic words had an unreal quality. She spoke them like a life-size puppet activated by strings and used by a voice that didn’t belong to her. Only her eyes were her own, and they contained a persistent stunned innocence.

There's really no reason to read this unless you really liked that sentence, or you're an 80 year old detective story fan. I enjoyed it, but I don't think I'll read anything else by this author.
